surfaces.part: dark back wall / opening above the stairs
wooden staircase body, seen face-on as stacked step bands
inner side panel / landing notch at right

answer.evidence: The body is a full-width wooden face from rows 14-46. It repeats 2-3 row light plank bands, each ending in a dark 1-2 row line at rows 16, 20-21, 27-28 and 36. Those bands read as vertical risers or planks. They are not depth-foreshortened treads: every band has the same width and there is no widening or receding of the silhouette (width is a constant 16 across rows 0-46). The dark block at rows 0-13 is a flat backdrop with no roof slope or lintel top surface. The stair treads and any roof or landing have no readable horizontal surface, so the drawing is a front elevation.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small wooden staircase prop, not a whole building with roof, walls and door. The references are two houses, so the comparison is only approximate. Its dark edge pixels are only 2% neutral, so the outlines lean brown and are tinted to the wood, which is good. It has no large flat fills (0% near-flat). It shows about 4 brown lightness steps on the wood, with stepped treads and risers, against about 6 steps per material on the references. It has 7 visible tones per tile against 10-12 for the references, and only 12 distinct colours in total against 66-185. There is little grain, no per-plank highlights or knots, and no speckle, so it looks thinner and flatter than the references. Since it is below both references on tones per tile and has less surface texture, and in case of doubt we fail, the verdict is fail.

surfaces.part: dark upper wall/opening above the stairs
wooden staircase body, drawn as stacked tread/riser stripes

answer.evidence: The staircase body (rows 14-46) is a flat face-on elevation. The column scan shows repeating 1-2 row light and dark stripes (rows 14-15, 16, 17-19, 20-21, 22-23, 26-28, 29-34) that read as tread and riser lines, not a foreshortened top plane. There is no ellipse, roof or slope plane, and no contents visible. Rows 0-13 are a uniform dark band with no edge line or eave shadow. The right-hand recess (rows 32-46) is a vertical outlined panel, not an isometric side face. The body therefore has no top surface and reads as front elevation.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small, narrow wooden stair piece, about one tile wide, set beside two full houses. It is drawn cleanly, but only 12 colours are used in total (7 per tile), against 185 and 66 for the references. It shows 7 visible tones per tile against 12 and 10, so it is clearly below both. Its dark edge pixels are only 2% neutral, so the outline is tinted dark brown and reads as a material tone rather than a black sticker line. Near-flat coverage is 0%, so there are no large flat fills. The wood has only about 4 lightness steps: a dark frame, a mid-brown tread and a lighter edge. It lacks the per-plank grain and speckle of the reference plaster, stone and tile work, and it reads thinner and flatter than the references. Because it is a sparse prop, I judged mainly by eye. I would not accept it next to the references without more tonal steps and texture, and since the rule is to fail when in doubt, I fail it.
